extracted.intended_audience: novice and new college mathematics instructors (instructor training coordinators running a pre‑semester orientation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and checklists for running a multi-block pre‑semester orientation for college mathematics instructors, including classroom practices, cooperative learning, quizzes, grading, homework teams, and practice teaching with videotaped feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Important features of sample lesson plans
rubrics_metrics.description: These important features may include: learning activities as part of the classroom; limits on the amount of lecturing; cooperative learning; use of calculators and technology to investigate mathematics; feedback and assessment items that are in harmony with course goals rather than working against course goals; lessons planned under the assumption that the students have read the textbook prior to class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize translating these features into instructor-created lesson plans. Use sample lesson plans in discussion and explicitly tie contents to course goals and a student-centered learning environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction to calculators / technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead a short presentation on the very basics of calculator usage such as calculator syntax for arithmetical calculations, basics of graphing, and using graphical calculation abilities to solve problems (for example, use a graphing calculator rather than calculus to solve a typical optimization problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have trainees practice short exercises in pairs. If your program uses CAS or other software, modify instructions appropriately. Alert instructors to a later in‑semester training that will focus on using technology meaningfully in support of course goals rather than re‑hashing basics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common evaluation techniques and grading scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe common evaluation techniques used in the department: exams, quizzes, homework, team homework, group projects, writing, portfolios, presentations, laboratory assignments; note any 'gateway' exams used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass out a sample grading scheme that weights components to obtain a final grade. Provide context about historical grade averages, institutional meanings of grades, and typical student interpretations. Emphasize having a well‑defined, well‑articulated grading scheme to hand out on the first day that should not be modified after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: First‑day outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize outcomes important to achieve on the first day of class, including: conveying all essential course information, requirements, and expectations; beginning to learn student names; beginning the process of students learning each other's names; creating an atmosphere for active learning; getting students into groups (if cooperative learning is to be regular); getting students to read the textbook before the next class; assigning homework (if regular); and doing some mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass out sample first‑day handouts and a student data form to support grouping and rapid familiarity. Encourage sharing of effective first‑day activities among trainers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for Meeting Block B (student-centered instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Block B goals: 1) Equip instructors with strategies for initial implementation of in‑class cooperative learning. 2) Alert instructors to possible difficulties in implementing in‑class cooperative learning. 3) Provide initial strategies for encouraging students to read the textbook. 4) Prepare instructors for designing a quiz policy that meaningfully supports course goals. 5) Prepare instructors for writing quizzes. 6) Assist instructors in articulating expectations to students concerning grading of collected items. 7) Equip instructors to form initial homework teams and convey procedures and roles to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these goals to structure the Block B meeting; note that items will be revisited in weekly in‑semester meetings for greater detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for Meeting Block B (materials and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare: 1) a brief activity instructors can do in groups while you model cooperative learning management; 2) a list of suitable in‑class cooperative learning activities for early weeks; 3) a packet of sample quizzes generated by department instructors; 4) a couple of student responses to typical assessment items (homework, quiz, exam) to use for grading practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a non‑mathematical activity for modeling to avoid competition among instructors; include sample student responses from the 'Meeting Materials' section if available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor capabilities required to implement in‑class cooperative learning
rubrics_metrics.description: To implement in‑class cooperative learning an instructor must be able to: quickly get students into groups; encourage them to start working rather than engage in off‑task discussion; interact with groups as they work; get students to stop and pay attention to the front at appropriate times; and wrap up the activity as a class and draw out the meaning before moving on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model group activities, role-play walking around and interacting with groups, and debrief with a class discussion to highlight these capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common problems in in‑class cooperative learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential difficulties include: some students passive/reluctant to participate; some students working on homework or other tasks instead of the assigned activity; off‑task conversations disrupting learning; some students dominating groups and dismissing contributions of others; cooperative activities take more time so coverage may be reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alert instructors to these issues and promise later training meetings with strategies to address them. Emphasize that, if implemented well, most students will be won over by increased learning and enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations in 'Getting Students to Read the Book' handout
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelve recommendations (repeated emphatically): 1–3 & 12: 'Don't lecture as if the students have never before seen the material!'; 4: You must really expect them to read the book and act as if you expect them to read it; 5: Set the tone the first day saying they must read the book and why; 6: You must read the book; 7: Make each day's reading assignment an event; 8: When you start the day's activities, do a brief activity that assumes the reading; 9: As a rule, don't do examples directly from the book unmodified (with exceptions); 10: When examples from the book are important/difficult, go over the hard parts and outline easier parts; 11: When they aren't doing the reading, try brief quizzes on the reading at the beginning of each day and group activities based on the reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated phrasing to set strong norms: model reading expectation through behavior and short lectures that preview or highlight reading. Use quizzes and group activities tied to reading to encourage compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals and rationales for giving quizzes
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible goals of quizzes include: to encourage attendance; to check if students have done homework and reading; to test basic competence with key skills; to test problem solving; to communicate instructor expectations in advance of exams; to provide regular feedback for both instructor and students on student progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have instructors articulate why they give quizzes because goals affect quiz design. Pass out sample quizzes and discuss grading/feedback. Always give useful feedback when grading and returning quizzes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quiz design considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Key questions for quiz design: Should questions be new or ones students have seen before? How long should quizzes be and how many points should each be worth? How often should quizzes be given? Should quizzes be announced or unannounced? How tough should quizzes be (adjust according to class morale)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide guidelines and be explicit that appropriate difficulty may vary; emphasize consistency with course goals and the importance of feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading practices and basic advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested grading basics: Don't nit‑pick—correct all errors but don't subtract points for every little error; give a number grade to each exercise rather than subtracting points (e.g., write '7' instead of '-3'); do not use emphatic markings when grading as they may demean students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out psychological effects of marks and the importance of conscientious grading. Recommend developing and using rubrics when grading papers to ensure consistency and to support regrade inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationales for homework teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework teams provide many of the same rationales as in‑class cooperative learning: a network of peers for consultation, a system of accountability, flexibility to require written reports on extensive problems/projects that would be prohibitive individually and for the instructor to grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss typical reactions, address reservations, and note that some students enjoy team work; consider prior team experience students bring from high school or other courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles in Homework Teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Team roles (rotate roles): Scribe (writes final version of homework to be graded; include symbolic, graphical, verbal explanations; neat/typed/stapled); Clarifier (paraphrases ideas, ensures everyone understands; most important role); Reporter (records meeting logistics, difficulties/successes, attendance, roles; report is first page of homework); Manager (arranges and runs meetings, ensures distribution of photocopies, can assume missing role if a team has only three members).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate roles each assignment so responsibilities are shared. Make explicit expectations about content, format, and reporting of attendance/roles on the homework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming initial homework teams
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: 1) Gather completed student data forms. 2) Collate forms into three piles according to first preference for team meeting time. 3) Put students within each pile into groups of four according to proximity on campus. 4) Make groups heterogeneous by gender, year, major, mathematical experience, ability, and attitudes where possible. 5) Move students between piles if necessary to accommodate meeting time preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use student data forms to facilitate logistics and heterogeneity. If homework teams will be formed later, consult additional handouts (e.g., 'Forming Homework Groups').

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for Block C: Practice teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Block C goals: 1) Provide instructors opportunity to practice organizing an explanation and presenting it. 2) Provide opportunity to receive feedback on presentation skills. 3) Provide opportunity to critically observe other teachers and consider applying observations to one's own teaching. 4) Organize visits by novice instructors to master teachers' classrooms early in the semester. 5) Provide trainers preliminary indications of areas for instructor development to target in in‑semester training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these goals to structure a longer session focused on mini‑lessons, videotaping, and peer feedback; ensure scheduling and follow‑up classroom visits are arranged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for Block C (logistics and equipment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare: find master teachers' schedules and secure cooperation for visits; arrange suitable rooms large enough for participants and video equipment (or multiple rooms with groups of 4–6 instructors and one trainer); ensure rooms have presentation devices instructors normally use (chalkboard, overhead projector, colored chalk/pens, graphing calculators, computers); ensure each room has videotaping and viewing equipment (video camera with good microphone and tripod; VCR and monitor; video cassette; stop‑watch or timer with audible alarm; copies of 'Guide for Evaluating Explanations'; name tags and writing materials; optional refreshments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be thoroughly familiar with operation of video equipment and be able to explain it quickly. Prepare problems/topics so each instructor presents different topics that can be handled in ~5 minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline and procedures for running Block C (mini‑lessons and feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: each instructor develops a mini‑lesson (no more than five minutes), is videotaped, and everyone watches clips using the 'Guide for Analyzing Explanations' to note effective points and suggestions. When giving feedback, begin with positive comments then move to suggestions. Timing breakdown suggested: 5–6 minutes watch clip, 1–2 minutes jot notes, 3–4 minutes instructor self‑comment, 6–7 minutes comments from others. Trainer must manage time carefully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stress strict time limits for mini‑lessons; encourage instructors who just finished to videotape the next person to reduce self‑focus; trainer should gently insist feedback begin with positives and focus comments to practical, concrete suggestions. Arrange classroom visits and feedback/reporting mechanisms (e.g., turn in 'Guide for Analyzing Explanations').

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide for Analyzing Explanations (rubric items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material and content items: 1) Instructor states the topic clearly at the beginning. 2) The explanation is organized. 3) Instructor emphasizes the main idea. 4) Instructor relates material to something students already know. 5) Instructor gives suitable examples. 6) Material is appropriate to level of beginning undergraduates. 7) Instructor has a clear conclusion. Technique and delivery items: 8) Instructor involves students. 9) Instructor shows enthusiasm. 10) Board work is clearly organized and readable. 11) Pace is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist while watching videotapes and during classroom observations; use comments section to record specifics. Use as a common vocabulary for feedback and for observational visit reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting materials required checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: List of meeting materials for the orientation: 1) copies of a course handbook; 2) an overhead outlining this training session and program; 3) an overhead outlining course goals; 4) copies of lesson plans for new instructors; 5) copies of sample first‑day handouts/syllabi; 6) copies of 'Student Data Form'; 7) copies of an activity to introduce in‑class cooperative learning; 8) copies of suggested in‑class cooperative learning exercises; 9) copies of 'Getting Students to Read the Book'; 10) copies of packet of sample quizzes; 11) photocopies of 'Student Responses to a Sample Problem' for grading; 12) copies of 'Roles in Homework Teams'; 13) copies of 'Forming Initial Homework Teams'; 14) copies of 'Guide for Analyzing Explanations'; 15) copies of 'Mathematics Teaching Orientation Session Evaluation Form.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute items in Blocks A–C as indicated and ensure trainers have all materials prepared prior to the session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an orientation session evaluation questionnaire
rubrics_metrics.description: Most training meetings suggest use of a questionnaire (see Appendix A). For the orientation session a specific 'Mathematics Teaching Orientation Session Evaluation Form' is provided and should be distributed to all instructors who attended the pre‑semester orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the questionnaire as a starting point for developing your own evaluation instrument; questions gather attendees' self‑rated experience level, which blocks they attended, and Likert responses about session components.
